tldr: In video prediction for dexterous manipulation, instead of leaving physical laws entirely to heavy video generation models, this work first explicitly predicts the rigid motion and deformation of objects using a lightweight 3D network before rendering. This prevents object shape collapse while achieving a massive speedup.
hero_caption: Concept and performance comparison of DeXplicit. (a) Models hand skeletal kinematics and object rigid motion / local deformation separately rather than using simple point trajectories; (b) Achieves ultra-fast video generation while maintaining high object region fidelity (IoU); (c) Prevents object disappearance and shape collapse seen in existing methods.
overview:
When a robot performs complex manipulation with its hands (dexterous manipulation), "world models" that predict how objects and the environment will change in response to hand motions are considered essential. However, existing approaches based on video generation models face a major pitfall: in pixel space, hand motion, object physical changes, camera viewpoint changes, and appearance texture synthesis are all intricately entangled. As a result, even if scenes look realistic at first glance, frequent issues occur where objects slip through palms, transform into entirely different shapes upon rotation, or vanish behind occlusions.

To address this, the authors asked: "Why not explicitly predict physical state evolution in 3D space before rendering visual consequences?" This led to their proposed method, "DeXplicit". In DeXplicit, a lightweight 3D dynamics network directly predicts the hand's joint structure, object rigid transformations (rotation and translation), and local deformations via an embedded graph in metric 3D space. Appearance texture features from the initial image are then transported along the predicted 3D motion and projected into future frames. This allows the video diffusion model to focus solely on completing uncertain areas and newly visible regions exposed by occlusions.

Evaluated on three benchmarks covering rigid, articulated, and deformable objects (HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin), DeXplicit reduced moved-point prediction error by 27–40% compared to an existing point-cloud world model (PointWorld). Furthermore, adapting it into a causal two-step generation model achieved a 57x speedup compared to their 14B bi-directional video generation configuration, demonstrating both collapse-free physical behavior and practical generation speeds.
contributions: Proposed a two-stage architecture that decouples the implicit learning of physical dynamics from video generation models, explicitly predicting object rigid transport and local deformation in metric 3D space.
Constructed a structured 3D dynamics network incorporating an articulation-aware action encoding for hand anatomy and an object-level pose correction adapter.

Introduced an appearance transport interface that projects initial frame features along predicted 3D point motion, selectively inpainting and rendering only unobserved regions using a prediction confidence soft mask.

Enabled high-quality object manipulation video generation at ultra-fast speeds (32 frames in 4.90 seconds) on a single GPU through a causal generation pipeline operating with just two steps per block and on-policy distillation.

sections.heading: Why shouldn't we leave physics solely to video generation models?
sections.summary: Conventional action-conditioned video generation models struggle to maintain contact relationships and object identity, even if their outputs look visually smooth. This section discusses the necessity of decoupling physical state evolution from visual rendering and placing metric 3D prediction first.
sections.details:
For robots to manipulate objects dexterously, they must accurately anticipate how their hand motions will alter the physical world and how the resulting scene will appear to a camera. While using video diffusion models as action-conditioned world models has gained traction recently, it faces a major hurdle: pixel-level visual plausibility does not equal physical correctness. Especially in fine-grained dexterous manipulation, even a slight misalignment in object pose causes contact breakdown.

When trying to predict future states directly in pixel space, hand motion, object physical behavior, camera viewpoints, lighting, and occlusions become completely entangled. As a result, drift occurs—such as objects being placed at incorrect 3D positions despite visually plausible grasps, or object shapes collapsing the moment they are hidden behind a hand. These problems stem from forcing the physical state to be captured implicitly inside the model's latent variables.

While attempts like PointWorld predict the world as point cloud trajectories, treating scenes as mere collections of points neglects geometric constraints such as the hand's hierarchical joint structure and coherent object-level rigid motion. DeXplicit proposes a clean separation: predicting physics explicitly in 3D, and rendering video by transporting appearance over that geometric scaffold.

sections.heading: At the intersection of world models, physics prediction, and video generation
sections.summary: This section organizes four related lineages: latent space dynamics, egocentric manipulation models, explicit physics simulators, and controllable video generation. DeXplicit's novelty lies in coupling measurable metric prediction with appearance transport.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of four major research areas:

### World Models for Manipulation
Approaches like the Dreamer family simulate environments in latent representations, while frameworks like UniPi and GR-1 connect video generation to robot policies. Foundation models with higher interactivity such as UniSim and Cosmos have also emerged, but they still cannot guarantee the geometric consistency demanded by dexterous manipulation.

### Dexterous Manipulation and Egocentric World Models
Models predicting egocentric hand interactions have been proposed, such as CosHand and InterDyn (which specify actions via hand masks or silhouettes) and DWM or Hand2World (which handle hand poses). However, these lack explicit physical object tracking and struggle to preserve object identity.

### Explicit Physical Dynamics Models
Fluid and rigid-body simulations using graph neural networks over point clouds or meshes (such as PointWorld and ParticleFormer) have the strength of operating directly on physical states. DeXplicit advances these by combining global object rigid motion (SE(3) transport) with an Embedded Graph for local deformation, providing a unified representation from rigid to deformable objects.

### Controllable Video Generation and Appearance Transport
Techniques for controlling diffusion models via external signals, such as ControlNet and CameraCtrl, are advancing rapidly. In particular, appearance transport—carrying texture features from initial frames forward along geometric paths—is drawing significant attention. DeXplicit distinguishes itself by binding this transport to accurate predicted 3D points, depth, and prediction confidence, inpainting only unobserved regions.

sections.heading: Problem setup: an elegant formulation from 3D prediction to video synthesis
sections.summary: The paper formulates the task of predicting future 3D states and video from an initial scene point cloud and hand action trajectories. The world model is decomposed into three components: a dynamics predictor, a projection operator, and a conditional renderer.
sections.details:
The task addressed in this work is to predict future metric 3D states and corresponding camera video while preserving object identity and texture, given initial scene observations and proposed future hand trajectories.

### Input Data
The inputs are an initial image $I^{0}$, an initial metric scene point cloud $X^{0}=\{x_{i}^{0}\}_{i=1}^{N}$, an anatomically indexed future hand trajectory $H^{0:T}$, and a calibrated camera matrix $\Pi$. Each object point $x_{i}$ is annotated with an object label $o_{i}$ and a canonical coordinate $c_{i}$ defined in the object's reference frame.

### Three-Stage Decomposition
DeXplicit decomposes this prediction process into three functions:
- Dynamics Predictor $F_{\theta}$: Predicts future 3D point positions $\widehat{X}^{1:T}$ and per-point confidence scores $Q^{1:T}$ from the initial point cloud and hand trajectory.
- Deterministic Projection Operator $\mathcal{R}$: Projects the predicted 3D geometry, confidence, initial appearance features, and hand poses onto the 2D image plane using camera matrices, constructing visual conditioning signal $C$ and soft mask $M$.
- Conditional Video Renderer $G_{\psi}$: Inpaints missing information and occluded regions based on the projected geometric scaffold and mask to generate the final RGB video.

sections.heading: Inside DeXplicit: structured 3D dynamics and confidence-gated rendering
sections.summary: The authors introduce an articulation-aware hand encoder, an object predictor separating rigid motion from local deformation, and a hand-candidate-based pose correction adapter. Appearance features are transported along 3D trajectories, and videos are synthesized using confidence masks.
sections.details:
The DeXplicit architecture consists of "Structured Interaction Dynamics" for accurate physical prediction and a "Confidence-Gated Visual Readout" for rendering it into video.

### 4.1 Structured Interaction Dynamics
Rather than moving point clouds arbitrarily, the model incorporates structural priors of hands and objects:
- Articulation-Aware Action Encoding: For the hand's 21 joints, relative positions from the wrist, displacements from the previous frame, and bone vectors connecting parent joints are constructed and encoded using a Transformer alongside joint types and hand identity (left/right) embeddings. MANO parameters (hand mesh coefficients) are also incorporated when available.
- Object-Centric Metric Dynamics: Initial point clouds are processed by a Point Transformer and pooled per object into object tokens. An object-temporal Transformer interacts with hand actions to predict object-level rigid rotation $R_o^t$ and translation $\tau_o^t$. To handle articulation and cloth deformation, $K$ control nodes are placed on the canonical object shape, and an Embedded Graph deformation network predicts per-node local transformations, which are composed with the rigid transform.
- Bounded Pose Correction: To fix initial estimation errors, a lightweight adapter predicts small local-frame twists (bounded within 5 cm translation and 15 degrees rotation), refining the final pose via the $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ exponential map.

### 4.2 Metric Alignment Refinement
To focus on reducing geometric errors in moving areas, a "moved-point objective" selects points with displacements exceeding 5 mm from the previous step, training on a combination of full-horizon, early-horizon, and endpoint losses. In addition, object candidate poses derived from bilateral hand rigid motions are provided as references, encouraging physically plausible pose updates.

### 4.3 Confidence-Gated Visual Readout
This interface converts 3D prediction results into imagery:
- Appearance Transport: The initial image $I^0$ is mapped into feature space using a pretrained VAE, and feature vectors are sampled at the projected coordinates of the initial point cloud. Each point retains this appearance feature as it moves to its future 3D position and is projected into the target camera view. This physically guarantees texture tracking across viewpoint changes and object motion.
- Confidence Gating: Point-level prediction confidence $Q$, computed from geometric uncertainty, is splatted onto the image plane to create a soft editing mask $M$. High-confidence regions (already visible textures) are preserved, directing the video diffusion model to render only hidden surfaces and geometrically uncertain regions.

sections.heading: Experimental results: massive boost in physics accuracy and an incredible 57x speedup
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across three major datasets: HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin. DeXplicit cut 3D moved-point error by up to 40% over PointWorld, substantially boosted object fidelity (IoU+) in video generation, and generated 32 frames in 4.90 seconds via causal generation.
sections.details:
To validate the method, extensive experiments were conducted on three datasets spanning rigid, articulated, and deformable object interactions (HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin).

### 5.1 Experimental Setup
As a baseline, PointWorld, a representative point-cloud world model, was retrained with the same 3D hand trajectories and initial point clouds. In video evaluation, in addition to image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), hand skeletal accuracy (PCK20), object overlap (IoU+), position error, and CLIP foreground similarity were used for multi-faceted evaluation.

### 5.2 Quantitative and Qualitative Results
- 3D Dynamics Prediction: In Table 1, DeXplicit reduced long-horizon moved-point error by 39.9% on HOT3D, 28.0% on OakInk2, and 27.1% on PhysTwin. As evident in Figure 4's qualitative results, PointWorld suffers from severe point scattering and fails to retain object shapes, whereas DeXplicit accurately captures bowls, laptop lids, and even deformations in cloth and rope.
- Conditional Video Generation: In a shared-renderer comparison, using PointWorld predictions as input achieved an object IoU+ of only 0.373, whereas DeXplicit input jumped by 47% to 0.549 (Table 2). Unlike existing methods (such as Hand2World) where objects vanish despite correct hand shapes, object identity and texture are preserved cleanly (Figure 5).
- Generation Efficiency (Speed): While a bi-directional 14B configuration took hundreds of seconds to generate video, introducing a causal adapter with 2-step denoising completed 32 frames in just 4.90 seconds (0.54 seconds for a 4-frame block), achieving a 57x speedup.

### 5.3 Ablation Study
Ablations confirmed that structured transport (explicit rigid motion) contributes most significantly to dynamics error reduction. For video generation, 3D geometric control, hand heatmaps, and appearance transport were each shown to progressively boost visual quality and object fidelity.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison of 3D dynamics prediction. Across rigid bodies (bowl, board), articulated objects (laptop opening/closing), and deformables (cloth, rope), PointWorld suffers from severe shape breakdown, while DeXplicit tracks accurately with extremely low end-point error (EPE).
captions.F5: Comparison of video generation results. When rotating boxes or manipulating bottles, existing video generation models alter object color and shape midway through, whereas DeXplicit (both standard and fast causal versions) completely preserves object identity.

sections.heading: Conclusion: the power of "3D first, rendering second" in dexterous manipulation
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that the simple design principle of explicitly predicting physical states in 3D before rendering dramatically improves both world model accuracy and generation efficiency.
sections.details:
This paper presented DeXplicit, an approach built on the clear principle that a dexterous manipulation world model should "first predict physical world evolution explicitly in 3D, and then synthesize visual appearance."

Decoupling complex physical law learning from visual rendering relieves video generation models of an excessive burden and enables geometrically consistent future state predictions. Furthermore, having this explicit 3D scaffold removes the need for heavy iterative denoising, unlocking ultra-fast video rendering with just two steps of causal inference. This represents a solid step toward building physically trustworthy robot world models.

sections.heading: Implementation and acceleration secrets: behind causal training and on-policy distillation
sections.summary: This section explains the three-stage training recipe (control learning, fast adapter, on-policy distillation) used to build the causal renderer, along with memory-efficient gradient computation techniques.
sections.details:
The appendix reveals the details of "Causal Post-Training," which underpins the model's high speed and stability (Figure F7).

### Training Stages for Fast Causal Generation
1. Stage 1 (Control Learning): Using a bi-directional Wan 1.3B model, conditioning adapters for projected geometry and appearance transport are trained via flow matching.
2. Stage 2 (Fast Adapter): Conditioning parameters are ported to a pretrained causal few-step model, aligning outputs using an endpoint reconstruction loss and a Video Critic.
3. Stage 3 (On-Policy Distillation): The student model performs rollouts conditioned on its own sequentially generated past frames (generated history), distilling toward velocity vectors from an EMA teacher model with cleaner history. Adding an adversarial loss from the Video Critic (adversarial weight 0.02) dramatically suppresses error accumulation and blurring during autoregressive inference (Figure F6).

### Gradient Computation under Memory Constraints
Unrolling causal slots while computing Video Critic gradients causes GPU memory to explode. To solve this, a memory-saving approach is introduced: a forward pass receives adversarial gradients at the latent leaf nodes, and gradients are accumulated by replaying slot by slot.

captions.F7: Three-stage training pipeline for the causal renderer. Proceeds from control learning with a bi-directional model (Stage 1), to fast adapter integration into a 2-step causal model (Stage 2), to on-policy distillation on self-generated history refined by a video GAN (Stage 3).
captions.F6: Ablation results for causal post-training. Simple teacher-forced flow matching or distillation alone leads to collapsed and blurry object shapes, whereas combining on-policy distillation with a Critic cleanly preserves shape and position.

takeaways: Expecting video diffusion models to memorize physical laws on their own is impractical; inserting metric 3D geometric prediction as an upfront scaffold is highly effective.

Rather than predicting unstructured point clouds, constraining dynamics by decomposing them into hand skeletal kinematics, object rigid motion (SE(3)), and local deformation graphs is key to physical accuracy.
With a solid 3D scaffold and appearance transport, the video generation side avoids collapse even with minimal 2-step denoising, achieving practical inference speeds on the order of seconds.
limitations: Assumes that accurate metric 3D point clouds (or depth) and future hand joint trajectories are provided upfront as initial inputs, requiring further validation regarding robustness against sensor noise.

Because appearance transport relies on textures observed in the initial frame, visual quality risks degrading on previously unobserved object backsides or large disoccluded regions exposed during manipulation.

While visually consistent futures can be predicted, strict contact dynamics as a physics engine (such as reaction forces and friction) are not guaranteed, meaning it cannot be deployed directly for safety-critical real-robot control.
